summary: Describes architecture and protocol requirements for controlling a Media Gateway from a Media Gateway Controller, the split used to connect telephone networks with Internet voice systems. It lays out what such a control protocol needs to do. It is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: A phone call going between old phone lines and the Internet needs a translator. This describes a boss that tells the translator what to do, and what language they must use to talk.

questions: what is a media gateway controller
subtitle: What a protocol for a call controller to command a media gateway must be able to do, from reserving resources to playing announcements.

tldr.problem: Voice and other media must cross between circuit-switched telephone networks and packet networks, and the gateways doing the conversion need a standard way to be controlled by a separate call-control element.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC does not define the protocol. It lists what the Media Gateway Control Protocol between a Media Gateway Controller (MGC) and a Media Gateway (MG) must support: per-call control, resource control, management, transport, security and bearer- and application-specific needs.
tldr.outcome: It served as the requirements checklist for the protocol work, which the text names as Megaco/H.248. It is an informational memo, not a standard.

facts.label: MGC span of control
facts.value: One MG to a few tens of thousands

today: RFC 2805 is an Informational memo from April 2000. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It states requirements rather than a protocol, and the text names Megaco/H.248 as the protocol context.

sections.title: Scope and Key Definitions
sections.content:
This RFC describes requirements for the Media Gateway Control Protocol, used between a Media Gateway Controller and a Media Gateway. The key words MUST, SHOULD and so on carry their RFC 2119 meanings and set the requirement level for the protocol.

  • Media Gateway (MG): does media mapping or transcoding between dissimilar networks, at least one of which is a packet, frame or cell network. It might terminate circuit-network trunks or loops, packetize the media and send it into a packet network, and do the reverse in the other direction.
  • Media Gateway Controller (MGC): controls an MG.
  • Signaling Gateway (SG): sends and receives native circuit-network signalling at the edge of a data network, for example relaying or terminating SS7.
  • Termination: a point where media flows enter or leave the MG, such as a DS0, an ATM VC or an RTP port. A connection associates terminations, typically two but possibly more.
  • Trunk and line (loop): the circuit-side connections, the first from a circuit switch and the second from a user terminal.

MGs are not limited to circuit-to-packet work. A conference bridge with all packet interfaces, an interactive voice response unit or an audio resource function can also be an MG.
sections.eli5: A gateway is a translator between the phone network and the Internet. The controller is the boss that tells it which calls to connect, and the connection points are called terminations.

sections.title: What the Gateway Is Assumed to Do
sections.content:
MGs can be built in many ways, so the protocol must not favour one architecture. For example, announcements could come from a media resource or from the termination itself, and the MGC must be able to send the identical request to two different implementations and get identical behaviour.

An MG is assumed to provide these functions:

  • reserving and releasing resources, and reporting their state;
  • maintenance operations such as loopbacks and continuity tests;
  • connection management, including connection state;
  • media processing such as transcoding and conferencing;
  • digit analysis and script interpretation for terminations;
  • event detection and signal insertion for per-channel signalling;
  • configuring signalling backhauls, and managing the MGC-MG association.

The MG may join two terminations of the same type, acting like a switch, so media conversion is not needed every time. The MG also keeps some control of its own resources, for example the RTP port number space.
sections.eli5: The rule is that the boss should not need to know how the translator is built inside. Ask two different translators the same thing, and you get the same result.

sections.title: Per-Call and Resource Requirements
sections.content:
Section 5 lists what the protocol must do for each call. Highlights:

  • Reservation: reserve bearer terminations and media resources for a call and release them, with a reservation staying in effect until the MGC explicitly releases it.
  • Connections: packet and circuit terminations in any combination (including "hairpin" connections inside one MG), unidirectional and bidirectional flows, multiple media types, point-to-multipoint, conferences, and adding or removing streams and participants during a call.
  • Media transformation: adapt between transports and encodings, invoke echo cancellation, and let the MGC choose how DTMF and other tones are handled (for example sent to the MGC, or carried in a separate RTP stream).
  • Events and signals: the MGC can enable or mask event reporting, set signals such as ringing, insert announcements, and download a script to run when an event occurs.
  • QoS, test and accounting: set and change QoS, support PSTN continuity testing, and collect per-media-flow start and stop times, volume and QoS statistics.

Section 6 covers resource control. The MG must report in-service and out-of-service changes, and there must be a discovery mechanism so an MGC can learn which resources an MG has. The MGC must be able to name an exact resource or use a wild card and let the MG choose, and DNS names and IP addresses must be usable to identify MGs and MGCs.
sections.eli5: The boss must be able to say: save a line for this call, connect these two ends, play a tone, tell me if someone presses a key, and keep count of how long it lasted.

sections.title: Reliability, Transport and Security Requirements
sections.content:
The protocol must let both sides detect and recover from loss of contact and from disagreement about resource and connection state, for example through audits. It must allow more than one backup MGC, an orderly switchback to the primary, and keeping already established connections when an MGC fails. It must also define a common, extensible MG MIB.

General requirements include being modular and extensible, supporting several operations in one message treated as one transaction, and putting a version identifier in the initial message exchange. It must scale from one termination to millions in an MG, and from one MG to a few tens of thousands under an MGC. It should also not rule out peak calling rates on the order of 140 calls per second on a moderately loaded network.

The continuity-test constraints are a maximum of 200ms cross-MGC IAM propagation delay and a maximum of 200ms from end of dialing to IAM emission.

The protocol must assume the underlying network may be a large shared network, does not assure reliable delivery, does not guarantee ordering and does not prevent duplicate transmissions. It must be able to abort delivery of obsolete messages, support priority messages, let each side correlate commands with responses, give a reason for any command failure, and keep one lost packet from stalling unrelated messages. The RFC itself notes that these needs might justify a separate reliable transport layer.

For security, mechanisms may come from the transport, such as IPSEC. The protocol or those mechanisms must allow mutual authentication at the start of an MGC-MG association, protect control messages once it is set up, offer optional confidentiality with a choice of algorithm, operate across untrusted domains, support non-repudiation for a customer-located MG talking to an operator's MGC, and mitigate denial of service attacks. Passing through commonly used firewalls is described as desirable. The RFC says the protocol document itself will need an extended security discussion.
sections.eli5: If the boss stops answering, the translator must know what to do, and messages can get lost or doubled. They also need to prove who they are, so nobody can pretend to be the boss.

sections.title: Bearer Types and Gateway Applications
sections.content:
Section 11 lists requirements by bearer type and by application. The protocol must support all bearer types in the RFC's Table 1, including trunk with ISUP, trunk with MF, ISDN, analogue, restricted-capability gateways, application terminations such as IVR, and multimedia H.323 and H.320.

  • TDM circuit: specify the encoding (for example mu-law or A-law), echo cancellation, rate adaptation, and a specific circuit or a circuit group from which the MG picks one.
  • Packet: specify coding, RTP and RTCP ports, RTP payload type, unicast or multicast, and encryption, with the MG able to allocate its own receive ports and report them.
  • ATM: address VCs, AAL2 slots and AAL1/AAL2/AAL5 details, and decouple the narrow-band connection from the VCC underneath.
  • Application types: trunking and access gateways, fax (T.38 or G.711), text telephones (T.140 in the packet network), network access servers, restricted-capability gateways, multimedia gateways and multipoint control units.

The NAS requirements include modem type, TDM data rate, rate adaptation, passing called and calling party numbers from the MGC, and directing the NAS to connect to a specific tunnel such as an LNS or an AAA server.
sections.eli5: Different gateways handle different things, like phone lines, fax machines, modems and conference calls. The protocol has to be able to describe all of them.

sections.title: Audio Resource Function Modules
sections.content:
The longest part of section 11 describes the Audio Resource Function (ARF), which can run on a stand-alone server or a traditional gateway. A gateway doing any of its modules is called an Audio Enabled Gateway. The modules are Play Audio, DTMF Collect, Record Audio, Speech Recognition, Speaker Verification/Identification, Auditory Feature Extraction/Recognition and Audio Conferencing.

Each later module must support everything in the Play module. Play Audio covers volume, speed, iterations, interval and duration, and playable segments such as recordings, text to speech, silence, tones and voice variables. Segments can be nested, and a set can be resolved by a qualifier such as language. DTMF Collect adds attempts, digit timers, prompt types (initial, reprompt, error, failure and success) and digit patterns given as a regular expression. Audio can be specified directly in the command or by an identifier that resolves to a provisioned sequence.
sections.eli5: This part is about the helper that talks to callers, like the voice that says a number is no longer in service and asks you to press keys.

items.title: Per-call
items.text: Reservation, connections, media transformations, events and signals, QoS, test and accounting.

items.title: Resource control
items.text: Status reporting, discovery and resource assignment.

items.title: Operations
items.text: Loss of contact, backup MGCs, error control and a common MIB.

items.title: Transport and security
items.text: Unreliable, unordered transport assumed; mutual authentication and protection of control messages.

items.title: Bearers and applications
items.text: TDM, packet and ATM bearers; trunking, access, NAS, fax, text, multimedia and audio resources.
